newsitem.title: JAPAN: Bank of Japan airs guarded concern about prices.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Japan airs guarded concern about prices.

text.p: Japan"s central bank sounded a note of guarded caution on Wednesday against a creeping rise in the price of goods in a country which has experienced zero inflation, even deflation, for the past four years.
Yasuo Matsushita, the governor of the Bank of Japan, told a news conference that domestic prices do not show any signs of moving into a clear upward trend.
"However, the weak yen has speeded up the tempo of the rise in prices of imports, and we need to watch domestic prices carefully from now on," he said.
Economists said there were valid reasons for the caution.
Some market operators speculated Matsushita may have made the remarks to make it easier for the central bank to raise short-term interest rates later this year.

"Until now, there have been no reasons to worry about the rekindling of inflation in Japan. But recent price moves certainly warrant vigilance and we are now at a turning point," said Yozo Nishimura, an economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.
The sharp fall of the yen against the dollar since mid-1995 has gradually pushed up import prices, and the pace of the decline in overall domestic prices has steadily slowed.
After hitting a record high of 79.75 to the dollar in April 1995, the yen has trodden a continuous downward path. The dollar was hovering around 124 yen in Tokyo on Wednesday.

The BOJ announced on Wednesday that import prices for the first 10 days of February rose 15.8 percent from February last year. Import prices have risen more than 10 percent on a year-on-year basis in the past three months.
Domestic wholesale prices fell a mere 0.3 percent in January after falls of 0.5 percent in December, 0.6 percent in November and 0.7 percent in October.
A Reuters poll of economists last month produced an average estimate for the rise in Japan"s wholesale prices in 1996 of 0.7 percent and a forecast of a 1.1 percent rise in 1997.
Some financial market operators said the BOJ may have started expressing its concern about inflation now so it can use it a reason later this year to rectify its super-accomodative monetary policy.
"I guess Mr. Matsushita made the remarks intentionally so the BOJ can raise short-term interest rates after the April-June quarter," said a bond dealer at a major Japanese securities house.
Financial markets widely believe the BOJ wants to increase market interest rates after it is assured that a planned rise of Japan"s sales tax on April 1 will not pull down the economy.

The BOJ has kept short-term interest rates at record-low levels since it cut the official discount rate -- a key lending rate -- to a record-low of 0.5 percent in September 1995 in a bid to give support to the flagging economy.
The central bank has traditionally tightened its monetary policy by raising the official discount rate to control inflation.
